prompt: Under the lesson’s idealised push-gossip model (synchronous one-second rounds, reliable delivery, uniform random peers and fanout 1), the leading-term estimate is about 17 seconds to reach all 1,000 nodes. If the cluster doubles to 2,000 nodes, what does the same estimate predict?

options.text: About twice as long, roughly 34 seconds, because there are twice as many nodes to tell.
options.explanation: Wrong. That is linear thinking. Every informed node also gossips, so the informed set grows multiplicatively and doubling the cluster costs only a round or two more.

options.text: Exactly the same time, because each node still contacts one peer per round.
options.explanation: Wrong. Fanout per node is unchanged, but there is one more doubling to do and a slightly longer tail, so it takes a little longer.

options.text: Only a second or two longer, because gossip rounds grow with the logarithm of the cluster size.
options.explanation: Correct. One extra round covers the extra doubling, and the slow tail grows only slightly (by about ln 2, under one round), so roughly 18–19 seconds.

options.text: It may never finish, because gossip cannot converge in large clusters.
options.explanation: Wrong. Gossip is designed for large clusters precisely because it converges in a number of rounds that grows only logarithmically.

workedExample:
Think about how the informed set grows.

1. Early on, everyone who knows tells someone new, so the informed set roughly **doubles** each round. Going from 1,000 to 2,000 nodes needs just **one more doubling**.
2. Near the end, random choices keep hitting nodes that already know, creating a slow tail. For push gossip that tail also grows only with the logarithm of the cluster size, so doubling the cluster adds well under one more round.
3. Total: from about 17 rounds to about 18–19 rounds, a second or two at one round per second.

Under the idealised model (synchronous rounds, reliable delivery, uniform random peers), the number of rounds grows as O(log N), where N is the number of nodes. Push-pull gossip shortens the tail further. Constant fanout is not constant bandwidth: message size still depends on how much state is exchanged.
